claim: With the availability of high-quality full genome polymorphism (SNPs) data, it becomes feasible to study the past demographic and selective history of populations in exquisite detail.
source: With the availability of high-quality full genome polymorphism (SNPs) data, it becomes feasible to study the past demographic and selective history of populations in exquisite detail.
evidence: This is a general statement about the capabilities enabled by SNP data availability, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Inferences of population history from SNPs suffer from a lack of statistical resolution for recent events, such as bottlenecks.
source: However, such inferences still suffer from a lack of statistical resolution for recent, for example bottlenecks, events, and/or for populations with small nucleotide diversity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations throughout the manuscript and represents a known limitation in the field.

claim: Additional heritable (epi)genetic markers, such as indels, transposable elements, microsatellites, or cytosine methylation, may provide further information on recent population history.
source: Additional heritable (epi)genetic markers, such as indels, transposable elements, microsatellites, or cytosine methylation, may provide further, yet untapped, information on the recent past population history.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential utility of additional markers, which is then tested in the study.

claim: The extended SMC framework can improve the accuracy of demographic inference in recent times.
source: We are able to (1) improve the accuracy of demographic inference in recent times, (2) uncover past demographic events hidden to SNP-based inference methods, and (3) infer the hyper-mutable marker mutation rates under a finite site model.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results and empirical analyses presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The extended SMC framework can uncover past demographic events hidden to SNP-based inference methods.
source: We are able to (1) improve the accuracy of demographic inference in recent times, (2) uncover past demographic events hidden to SNP-based inference methods, and (3) infer the hyper-mutable marker mutation rates under a finite site model.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations and application to A. thaliana data showing bottlenecks not detected by SNP-only methods.

claim: The extended SMC framework can infer hyper-mutable marker mutation rates under a finite site model.
source: We are able to (1) improve the accuracy of demographic inference in recent times, (2) uncover past demographic events hidden to SNP-based inference methods, and (3) infer the hyper-mutable marker mutation rates under a finite site model.
evidence: This is supported by Table 1 showing accurate estimation of mutation rates across different values.

claim: Segregating single methylated polymorphisms (SMPs) satisfy the modeling assumptions of the SMC framework.
source: We demonstrate that segregating single methylated polymorphisms (SMPs) satisfy the modeling assumptions of the SMC framework, while differentially methylated regions (DMRs) are not suitable as their length exceeds that of the genomic distance between two recombination events.
evidence: This is supported by analyses of LD decay and distribution statistics shown in Figure 4.

claim: Differentially methylated regions (DMRs) are not suitable for SMC analysis because their length exceeds the genomic distance between two recombination events.
source: We demonstrate that segregating single methylated polymorphisms (SMPs) satisfy the modeling assumptions of the SMC framework, while differentially methylated regions (DMRs) are not suitable as their length exceeds that of the genomic distance between two recombination events.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing DMR lengths to genealogy spans in Figure 4B, showing DMRs are on average twice as large.

claim: The SMC framework provides new estimates of the glacial age bottleneck and post-glacial population expansion of the European A. thaliana population.
source: Combining SNPs and SMPs while accounting for site- and region-level epimutation processes, we provide new estimates of the glacial age bottleneck and post-glacial population expansion of the European A. thaliana population.
evidence: This is supported by the demographic inference results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The SMC framework readily accounts for a wide range of heritable genomic markers.
source: Our SMC framework readily accounts for a wide range of heritable genomic markers, thus paving the way for next-generation inference of evolutionary history by combining information from several genetic and epigenetic markers.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations with different marker types and mutation rates throughout the manuscript.

claim: SMC, DL, or ABC inference methods aim to infer demographic changes and signatures of selection directly from full genome sequencing data.
source: Inference methods based on deep learning (DL, Korfmann et al., 2023), approximate Bayesian computation (ABC, Boitard et al., 2016), or sequential Markovian coalescent (SMC, Li and Durbin, 2011; Schiffels and Durbin, 2014) aim to infer this information directly from full genome sequencing data, which is becoming rapidly available for many (non-model) species due to decreasing costs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant methodological papers.

claim: The SMC offers an elegant theoretical framework that builds on the classical Wright-Fisher and the backward-in-time Kingman coalescent stochastic models.
source: The SMC, in particular, offers an elegant theoretical framework that builds on the classical Wright-Fisher and the backward-in-time Kingman coalescent stochastic models (e.g. Kingman, 1982; Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 2010; Wakeley, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational theoretical work.

claim: The Kingman coalescent model conceptualizes Mendelian inheritance as generating the genealogy of a population.
source: Both models conceptualize Mendelian inheritance as generating the genealogy of a population (or a sample), that is, the unique history of a fragment of DNA passing from parents to offspring.
evidence: This is a fundamental concept in coalescent theory supported by the cited references.

claim: When the genealogy includes the effect of recombination, it is called the ancestral recombination graph (ARG).
source: When this genealogy includes the effect of recombination, it is called the ancestral recombination graph (ARG, Hudson, 1983; Wiuf and Hein, 1999).
evidence: This is a standard definition in population genetics supported by citations.

claim: The true genealogy of a population contains information on past demographic changes and life history traits.
source: Under the Kingmann coalescent model, the true genealogy of a population (or sample) is defined by its topology and branch length, and contains the information on past demographic changes and life history traits (Nordborg, 2000; Sellinger et al., 2020; Strütt et al., 2023; Tellier et al., 2011) as well as selective events (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 2010; Wakeley, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to theoretical and empirical work.

claim: The genealogical and mutational processes of any heritable marker can be disentangled.
source: The genealogical and the mutational processes of any heritable marker can, therefore, be disentangled, and the frequency of any given marker state is given by the shape of the genealogy in time (see Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a theoretical principle illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: A central assumption about heritable genomic markers is that they are generated by two homogeneous Poisson mutation processes along the genome and through time.
source: A central assumption about heritable genomic markers is that they are generated by two homogeneous Poisson mutation processes along the genome as well as through time.
evidence: This is a fundamental modeling assumption in coalescent theory.

claim: Mutations in different genealogies are independent due to the effect of recombination.
source: This entails that mutations in different genealogies are independent due to the effect of recombination (Wiuf and Hein, 1999; McVean and Cardin, 2005), and that there are no time periods with a large excess, or a severe lack, of mutations along a genealogy (mutations are independently distributed in time within a DNA fragment).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work on recombination and mutation.

claim: Model violations such as variation in recombination and mutation rates along the genome can compromise the accuracy of demographic and selective inference.
source: Despite the power of the SMC, well-known model violations such as variation in recombination and mutation rates along the genome (Barroso et al., 2019; Barroso and Dutheil, 2023) or pervasive selection (Schraiber and Akey, 2015; Johri et al., 2021; Johri et al., 2020) can compromise the accuracy of demographic and selective inference (Gattepaille et al., 2013; Sellinger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies documenting these issues.

claim: Inferences can be biased when the population recombination rate (ρ) is higher than the population mutation rate (θ).
source: The first issue occurs when the population recombination rate (ρ) is higher than the population mutation rate (θ). In such cases, inferences can be biased if not erroneous (Terhorst et al., 2017; Sellinger et al., 2021; Sellinger et al., 2020), because several recombination events cannot be inferred due to the lack of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs for point mutations).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this bias.

claim: The typical low mutation rate of 10^-9 up to 10^-8 per base per generation places strong limitations on SMC analysis of recent bottleneck events.
source: The typical low mutation rate of 10−9 up to 10−8 (per base, per generation) found in most species, therefore, places strong limitations on SMC analysis of recent bottleneck events (up to ca. 104 generations ago) when inference is based solely on SNP data.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between mutation rates and temporal resolution.

claim: Bottlenecks are often either not found, or when inferred, their timing and magnitude are not well estimated.
source: Indeed, bottlenecks are often either not found, or when inferred, their timing and magnitude are not well estimated (inferred smoother than in reality, Johri et al., 2021; Sellinger et al., 2021), even when a large number of samples is used.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies documenting these limitations.

claim: Current SMC, DL, or ABC inference methods rely almost exclusively on SNPs for inference.
source: Nonetheless, current SMC, DL, or ABC inference methods making use of full genome sequence data rely almost exclusively on SNPs for inference (Schiffels and Durbin, 2014; Terhorst et al., 2017; Sellinger et al., 2020; Boitard et al., 2016; Korfmann et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to major inference methods.

claim: SNPs are easily detectable from short-read re-sequencing data.
source: There are both practical and theoretical reasons for using SNPs: They are easily detectable from short-read re-sequencing data and their mutational process is well approximated by the infinite site model (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 2010; Wakeley, 2008), simplifying the inference of the underlying genealogy.
evidence: This is a known practical advantage of SNPs in genomic studies.

claim: The mutational process of SNPs is well approximated by the infinite site model.
source: There are both practical and theoretical reasons for using SNPs: They are easily detectable from short-read re-sequencing data and their mutational process is well approximated by the infinite site model (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 2010; Wakeley, 2008), simplifying the inference of the underlying genealogy.
evidence: This is a standard theoretical assumption supported by citations.

claim: Other heritable genomic markers exist whose mutation rates can be several orders of magnitude higher than that of SNPs.
source: However, other heritable genomic markers exist whose mutation rates can be several orders of magnitude higher than that of SNPs and could thus be more informative about recent demographic events.
evidence: This is supported by known mutation rates of microsatellites, TEs, and methylation sites.

claim: Current technological limitations impede the easy detection and estimation of allele frequencies for many heritable markers.
source: Current technological limitations still impede the easy detection and estimation of allele frequencies for many of these markers (Yang et al., 2018; Ou et al., 2019; Wang, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on marker detection challenges.

claim: Identifying insertion/excision variation of transposable elements or copy number variation of microsatellites requires a high-quality reference genome and ideally long-read sequencing approaches.
source: For example, identifying insertion/excision variation of transposable elements or copy number variation of microsatellites requires a high-quality reference genome and ideally long-read sequencing approaches (Ou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on TE detection methods.

claim: DNA cytosine methylation is emerging as a potentially useful epigenetic marker for phylogenetic inference in plants.
source: In addition to these genomic markers, DNA cytosine methylation is emerging as a potentially useful epigenetic marker for phylogenetic inference in plants (Yao et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies on methylation-based phylogenetics.

claim: Stochastic gains and losses of DNA methylation at CG dinucleotides arise at a rate of ca. 10^-4 up to 10^-3 per site per generation.
source: Stochastic gains and losses of DNA methylation at CG dinucleotides, in particular, arise at a rate of ca. 10−4 up to 10−3 per site per generation (that is 4–5 orders of magnitude faster than DNA point mutations, van der Graaf et al., 2015), and can be inherited across generations (Pisupati et al., 2023; Weigel and Colot, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies measuring epimutation rates.

claim: CG methylation changes occur 4-5 orders of magnitude faster than DNA point mutations.
source: Stochastic gains and losses of DNA methylation at CG dinucleotides, in particular, arise at a rate of ca. 10−4 up to 10−3 per site per generation (that is 4–5 orders of magnitude faster than DNA point mutations, van der Graaf et al., 2015), and can be inherited across generations (Pisupati et al., 2023; Weigel and Colot, 2012).
evidence: This is calculated from the cited epimutation and mutation rates.

claim: Spontaneous epimutations are likely neutral at the genome-wide scale.
source: These so-called spontaneous epimutations are likely neutral at the genome-wide scale (Vidalis et al., 2016; Johannes and Schmitz, 2019b, but see Muyle et al., 2021; Pisupati et al., 2023), and can be easily detected from bisulphite converted short read sequencing data (Lister et al., 2008; Schmitz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on epimutation neutrality, with caveats noted.

claim: CG methylation data can be used as a molecular clock for timing divergence between pairs of lineages over timescales ranging from years to decades.
source: Recent work suggests that CG methylation data can be used as a molecular clock for timing divergence between pairs of lineages over timescales ranging from years to decades (Yao et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study demonstrating this application.

claim: The mutational process at hyper-mutable markers is reversible and more consistent with a finite site model.
source: Because of the high mutation rate, the mutational process at these (hyper-mutable) markers is reversible and more consistent with a finite site, rather than infinite site, model, which can result in extensive homoplasy (as known for microsatellite markers, Estoup et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a theoretical inference supported by a citation to work on microsatellites.

claim: Classic expectations of population genetics diversity statistics need to be revised for hyper-mutable markers.
source: Indeed, classic expectations of population genetics diversity statistics, mostly built for SNPs, need to be revised for these hyper-mutable markers (Charlesworth and Jain, 2014; Wang and Fan, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work on hyper-mutable markers.

claim: With the inclusion of hyper-mutable marker 2, SMCtheo correctly infers the rapid change of population size of the bottleneck.
source: However, with the inclusion of hyper-mutable marker 2, our SMCtheo approach correctly infers the rapid change of population size of the bottleneck (Figure 2A, green).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A where the green line accurately captures the bottleneck.

claim: Accurate estimation of demography is obtained even when the mutation rate of marker 2 is unknown.
source: It is encouraging that an accurate estimation of the demography is obtained, even when the mutation rate of marker 2 is unknown (Figure 2A, blue).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2A where the blue line shows good demographic inference.

claim: In the absence of hyper-mutable marker 2, no approach can correctly infer variation of population size when the effective population size is small (N=1,000).
source: We find that in the absence of the hyper-mutable marker 2, no approach can correctly infer the variation of population size.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B where methods using only marker 1 fail to detect the bottleneck.

claim: When integrating both markers, population size can be recovered even if the mutation rate of marker 2 is not a priori known.
source: Yet, when integrating both markers, the population size can be recovered, even if the mutation rate of marker 2 is not a priori known.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B where both green and blue lines recover the bottleneck.

claim: A very small proportion (0.1%) of hyper-mutable genomic sites is sufficient to significantly improve the accuracy of inferences.
source: This suggests that a very small proportion of hyper-mutable genomic sites is sufficient to significantly improve the accuracy of inferences.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing improved inference with only 0.1% marker 2 sites.

claim: By integrating genomic marker 2 which mutation rate is larger than the recombination rate, estimates of the recombination rate and past population size variation are substantially improved.
source: Our results show that by integrating the genomic marker 2 which mutation rate is larger than the recombination rate, estimates of the recombination rate as well as past population size variation are substantially improved (Table 2, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Table 2 and Figure 2C showing improved parameter estimates.

claim: The true recombination rate can be recovered well even with marker 1 only by directly optimizing the likelihood.
source: However, by directly optimizing the likelihood, the true recombination rate can be recovered well even with marker 1 only.
evidence: This is shown in Table 2 where the LH method with 1 marker estimates 0.84×10^-7 compared to the true value of 10^-7.

claim: SMCm can accurately recover site- and region-level epimutation rates except when these are higher than 10^-4.
source: Our SMCm approach can accurately recover these rates except when these are higher than 10-4.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Supplementary file 1c and d showing estimation accuracy.

claim: When epimutation rates are very high (close to 10^-2), accuracy is lost compared to slower epimutation rates.
source: Similar to our previous observation, we find that when the epimutation rates are very high (e.g. close to 10-2), accuracy is lost compared to slower epimutation rates.
evidence: This is shown in Supplementary file 1e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Average estimated epimutation rates are off from the true value by less than a factor of 10 when rates are very high.
source: Nonetheless, our average estimated rates are off from the true value by less than a factor 10.
evidence: This is inferred from the results in Supplementary file 1e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is virtually no linkage disequilibrium (LD) between epimutations due to the high epimutation rate.
source: There is virtually no linkage disequilibrium (LD) between epimutations due to the high epimutation rate (Figure 4C), while the LD between SNPs can range over few kbp (Figure 4D, as observed in A. thaliana [Cao et al., 2011; Schmitz et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4C showing rapid LD decay for epimutations.

claim: The LD between SNPs can range over few kbp in A. thaliana.
source: There is virtually no linkage disequilibrium (LD) between epimutations due to the high epimutation rate (Figure 4C), while the LD between SNPs can range over few kbp (Figure 4D, as observed in A. thaliana [Cao et al., 2011; Schmitz et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and supported by citations to A. thaliana studies.

claim: The simulator generates SNPs, SMPs, and DMRs which fulfill the three key assumptions from Figure 1A.
source: In other words, our simulator generates SNPs, SMPs, and DMRs, which fulfil the three key assumptions from Figure 1A.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the LD and distribution analyses in Figure 4.

claim: When the site epimutation rates are a priori known, the sharp decrease of population size can be accurately detected.
source: When the site epimutation rates are a priori known, the sharp decrease of population size can be accurately detected.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B where the demographic inference accurately captures the bottleneck.

claim: When epimutation rates are unknown, the shape of past demographic history is well inferred except for a scaling issue.
source: When epimutation rates are unknown, the shape of the past demographic history is also well inferred except for a scaling issue (a shift along the x- and y-axes similar to that in Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A showing good shape recovery with some scaling differences.

claim: Having methylation measurements for as low as 2% of all CG sites is sufficient to improve SNP-based demographic inference.
source: This suggests that having methylation measurements for as low as 2% of all CG sites being epimutable in the genome is entirely sufficient to improved SNP-based demographic inference (eSMC2 in Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A and B where 2%, 10%, and 20% methylation sites yield similar improvements.

claim: Incorporating SMPs with known site-level epimutations leads to substantial inference improvements when sequence length is reduced to 10 Mb.
source: However, incorporating SMPs with known site-level epimutations into the model leads to substantial inference improvements (Figure 5C, D, Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and D where SMCm outperforms eSMC2 with limited data.

claim: Integrating epimutations slightly improves the accuracy of TMRCA when the epimutation rates are known.
source: We confirm our intuition that integrating epimutations slightly improves the accuracy of TMRCA when the epimutation rates are known but does not when the rates are unknown.
evidence: This is quantified in Supplementary file 1g showing RMSE values for TMRCA inference.

claim: A gain of accuracy is observed when integrating DMR data with known epimutation rates.
source: As in Figure 5, we observed a gain of accuracy in inference when region-level epimutation rates are known, while the length of the region (1 kb or 150 bp) does not seem to affect the result.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: No significant gain of information is observed when integrating DMR data with unknown epimutation rates.
source: However, no significant gain of information is observed when integrating DMR data with unknown epimutation rates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and 2 where unknown rates don't improve inference.

claim: CG methylation SMPs and to a lesser extent DMRs can be used jointly with SNPs to improve demographic inference, especially in recent times.
source: In summary, CG methylation SMPs and to a lesser extend DMRs, can be used jointly with SNPs to improve demographic inference (Supplementary file 1h presents the corresponding RMSE values for demographic inference shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), especially in recent times (Supplementary file 1f and h).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by multiple simulation results and RMSE calculations.

claim: When epimutation rates are unknown, there is a gain of accuracy when integrating epimutations, especially in recent times.
source: When the epimutations rates are unknown, we observe a gain of accuracy when integrating epimutations, especially in recent times.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 for simulations with both site and region epimutations.

claim: When epimutation rates are a priori known, there is a loss of accuracy when accounting for epimutations in the presence of both site and region processes.
source: However, when epimutation rates are a priori known, we observe a loss of accuracy when accounting for epimutations.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and explained by mislabeling of methylation region status.

claim: The loss of accuracy when epimutation rates are known is due to mislabeling of the methylation region status when site and region-level epimutations occur jointly at similar rates.
source: This loss of accuracy is due to the mislabeling of the methylation region status (in step 1) when site and region-level epimutations occur jointly at similar rates (as there will be methylated sites in unmethylated regions and unmethylated sites in methylated regions).
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of the algorithm and the observed results.

claim: Ignoring site or region-level processes can decrease the accuracy of inference.
source: We show that (1) using SMPs we can unveil past demographic events hidden by limitations in SNPs, (2) the correct demography can be uncovered irrespective of knowing a priori the epimutation rates, (3) ignoring site or region-level processes can decrease the accuracy of inference, and (4) knowing the epimutation rates may improve the estimate of demography compared to simultaneously estimating them with SMCm.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 4 showing decreased accuracy when region effects are ignored.

claim: For all 10 individual A. thaliana methylomes, the hypothesis of a binomial distribution of methylated and unmethylated sites along the genomes is rejected.
source: As expected from Denkena et al., 2021, for all 10 individual full methylomes, we reject the hypothesis of a binomial distribution of methylated and unmethylated sites along the genomes, suggesting the existence of region effect methylation (yielding DMRs), meaning that CG are more likely to be methylated if in a highly methylated region, and conversely for unmethylated CG.
evidence: This is a statistical test result from the A. thaliana data analysis.

claim: The average p-value is smaller than 0.05 for distances up to 2,000 bp between CG methylation sites in A. thaliana.
source: We observe an average p-value smaller than 0.05 for distances up to 2,000 bp but then the p-value rapidly increases (>0.4) (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5 plotting p-values against distance.

claim: The HMM yields a DMR average length of 222 bp in A. thaliana.
source: As a second measure, our HMM (based on pairs of genomes) yields a DMR average length of 222 bp (distribution in Figure 4B).
evidence: This is calculated from the A. thaliana data and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The minimum distance for epimutations to be independent along a genome is over 2 kb in A. thaliana.
source: We conclude that the minimum distance for epimutations to be independent along a genome is over 2 kb and spans larger distances than the typically proposed DMR size (ca. 150 bp in Denkena et al., 2021 and 222 bp in our analysis) and can therefore cover the size of a gene (see Muyle et al., 2021; Briffa et al., 2023).
evidence: This is inferred from the p-value analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: The epimutation processes that produce DMRs at the population level in plants cannot simply result from the cumulative action of single-site epimutations.
source: The simulations and data from A. thaliana indicates that the epimutation processes that produce DMRs at the population level in plants cannot simply result from the cumulative action of single-site epimutations.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing simulations with only site-level epimutations to observed data patterns.

claim: The autocorrelation in CG methylation is a function of cooperative methylation maintenance and the distribution of histone modifications.
source: This insight is consistent with recent analyses of epimutational processes in gene bodies, which seems to indicate that the autocorrelation in CG methylation is a function of cooperative methylation maintenance and the distribution of histone modifications (Briffa et al., 2023; Lyons et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent mechanistic studies.

claim: DMRs are, on average, twice as large as the inferred genomic genealogy span in A. thaliana: average length of 222 bp (DMR) vs 137 bp (genealogy).
source: We observe that both distributions have a similar shape, but DMRs are, on average, twice as large as the inferred genomic genealogy span: average length of 222 bp (DMR) vs 137 bp (genealogy) and median length of 134 bp (DMR) vs 62 bp (genealogy).
evidence: This is calculated from the distributions shown in Figure 4B.

claim: On average, DMRs are larger than the average distance between two recombination events in A. thaliana, violating the homogeneous distribution of epimutations along the genome.
source: This means that, on average, DMRs are larger than the average distance between two recombination events, thus violating the homogeneous distribution of epimutations along the genome (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of DMR and genealogy span distributions in Figure 4B.

claim: The LD between SMPs in A. thaliana data is high for distances smaller than 100 bp.
source: We find the LD between SMPs in the data to be high (and higher than LD between SNPs) for distances smaller than 100 bp (red line in Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C comparing LD decay between data and simulations.

claim: The LD decay of SMPs is much faster than for SNPs in A. thaliana.
source: The LD decay of SMPs is much faster than for SNPs (no linkage disequilibrium between epimutations for distances >100 bp), likely stemming from (1) epimutation rates being much higher than the DNA mutation rate, and (2) the high per-site recombination rate in A. thaliana.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 4C and D and explained by known rate differences.

claim: The LD between SMPs at distances smaller than 100 bp in A. thaliana is much higher compared to simulations.
source: Moreover, the LD between SMPs at distances smaller than 100 bp in A. thaliana being much higher compared to our simulations (Figure 4C), we suggest that additional local mechanisms of epimutation processes may not be accounted for in our model of the region-level methylation process.
evidence: This is observed by comparing red and blue lines in Figure 4C.

claim: When using SNP data only, the demographic results for A. thaliana are similar to those previously found, with no strong evidence for an expansion post-Last Glacial Maximum.
source: When using SNP data only, the demographic results are similar to those previously found (Sellinger et al., 2020; Strütt et al., 2023; Figure 6 purple lines), with no strong evidence for an expansion post-Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) (Cao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 (purple lines) and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: When using empirically inferred methylation and demethylation rates, a mild bottleneck post-LGM is followed by recent expansion in A. thaliana.
source: When we use as input the methylation and demethylation rates that have been inferred experimentally (van der Graaf et al., 2015), a mild bottleneck post-LGM is followed by recent expansion (Figure 6 blue lines).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 (blue lines) using fixed epimutation rates.

claim: When SMCm estimates the epimutation rates, a strong bottleneck event occurs between ca. 5,000 and 10,000 generations ago in A. thaliana, followed by an expansion until today.
source: By contrast, letting our SMCm estimate the epimutation rates, we find in recent times a somehow similar but stronger demographic change post-LGM. We find a strong bottleneck event occurring between ca. 5,000 and 10,000 generations ago, followed by an expansion until today (Figure 6 green lines).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 (green lines) when epimutation rates are estimated.

claim: The inferred site epimutation rates in A. thaliana are 10,000 times faster than the DNA mutation rate.
source: The inferred site epimutation rates are 10,000 faster than the DNA mutation rate (Supplementary file 1k), which is close to the expected order of magnitude from experimental measures with and without DMR effects (van der Graaf et al., 2015; Denkena et al., 2021).
evidence: This is calculated from the inferred rates in Supplementary file 1k and compared to experimental measures.

claim: The inclusion of DNA methylation data can aid in the accurate reconstruction of the evolutionary history of populations, particularly in the recent past.
source: These results indicate that the inclusion of DNA methylation data can aid in the accurate reconstruction of the evolutionary history of populations, particularly in the recent past, where SNPs reach their resolution limit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the A. thaliana analysis results in Figure 6.

claim: DNA methylation status at CG dinucleotides undergoes stochastic changes at rates several orders of magnitude higher than the DNA mutation rate and can be inherited across generations.
source: This is made possible by the fact that the DNA methylation status at CG dinucleotide undergoes stochastic changes at rates that are several orders of magnitude higher than the DNA mutation rate and can be inherited across generations similar to DNA mutations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies on epimutation rates and heritability.

claim: By integrating multiple heritable genomic markers, population size variation in very recent time can be more accurately recovered.
source: We demonstrate that by integrating multiple heritable genomic markers, the population size variation in very recent time can be more accurately recovered (outperforming any other methods given the amount of data used in this study [Terhorst et al., 2017; Speidel et al., 2019]).
evidence: This is demonstrated throughout the Results section with various simulation scenarios.

claim: Correctly integrating multiple genomic markers can improve TMRCA inference.
source: Our results indicate that correctly integrating multiple genomic marker can improve TRMCA inference, which is becoming a field of high interest (Korfmann et al., 2024; Hubisz et al., 2020; Mahmoudi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by RMSE calculations in Supplementary file 1g and citations to relevant work.

claim: If the SNP mutation rate is known, the mutation rate of other markers can be recovered under the condition that the marker follows all hypotheses described in Figure 1.
source: Our simulations demonstrate that if the SNP mutation rate is known, the mutation rate of other markers can be recovered (under the condition that the marker follow all hypotheses described in Figure 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Table 1 showing accurate mutation rate estimation.

claim: The method accounts for the finite site problem that arises at reversible (hyper-mutable) markers and/or where effective population size is high.
source: Moreover, our method accounts for the finite site problem that arises at reversible (hyper-mutable) markers and/or where effective population size is high (Tellier et al., 2011; Upadhya and Steinrücken, 2022).
evidence: This is a design feature of the method supported by citations to relevant theoretical work.

claim: Comparisons of LD for different markers along the genome is a useful way to assess violations of model assumptions.
source: We find that comparisons of LD for different markers along the genome is a useful way to assess violations of our model assumptions.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4C and D where LD patterns reveal model violations.

claim: A. thaliana presents the largest genetic and epigenetic data-set of high quality.
source: Indeed, A. thaliana presents the largest genetic and epigenetic data-set of high quality.
evidence: This is a known fact about A. thaliana as a model organism.

claim: The methylation state in CG context in A. thaliana is mainly heritable and well documented.
source: Additionally, the methylation states in CG context has been proven mainly heritable and is well documented (Denkena et al., 2021; Hazarika et al., 2022; van der Graaf et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies on CG methylation heritability.

claim: The model-based approach provides strong evidence that DMRs cannot simply emerge from spontaneous site-level epimutations that arise according to Poisson processes along the genome.
source: Our model-based approach provides strong evidence that DMRs cannot simply emerge from spontaneous site-level epimutations that arise according to a Poisson processes along genome.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing model predictions to observed data patterns.

claim: Stochastic changes in region-level methylation states must be the outcome of spontaneous methylation and demethylation events that operate at both the site- and region-level.
source: Instead, stochastic changes in region-level methylation states must be the outcome of spontaneous methylation and demethylation events that operate at both the site- and region-level (as corroborated by Pisupati et al., 2023; Briffa et al., 2023; Lyons et al., 2023).
evidence: This is inferred from the data analysis and supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The epimutation model cannot fully describe the observed diversity of epimutations along the genome.
source: Our epimutation model cannot fully describe the observed diversity of epimutations along the genome (Denkena et al., 2021), meaning that the epimutation processes may indeed be more complex than expected (Denkena et al., 2021; Hazarika et al., 2022; Briffa et al., 2023; Lyons et al., 2023).
evidence: This is inferred from discrepancies between model predictions and observed data.

claim: Non-independence is observed between annotated methylation sites spanning genomic regions larger than the span of the underlying genealogy in A. thaliana.
source: We observe non-independence between annotated methylation sites spanning genomic regions larger than the span of the underlying genealogy (determined by recombination events) which no model can currently describe.
evidence: This is observed from the p-value analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Methylation probably violates the assumptions of a Poisson process distribution along the genome and in time.
source: Thus, methylation probably violate the assumptions of a Poisson process distribution along the genome and in time (i.e. Figure 1), in line with recent functional studies (Pisupati et al., 2023; Hazarika et al., 2022; Lyons et al., 2023).
evidence: This is inferred from observed LD patterns and supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Caution is warranted against conclusions on the role of natural selection based on population epigenomic data due to violation of model assumptions.
source: We thus further caution against conclusions on the role of natural (purifying) selection (Muyle et al., 2021) or its absence (Vidalis et al., 2016) based on population epigenomic data due to the violation of the above-mentioned assumptions.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement based on the observed model violations.

claim: The discrepancy between inferred and experimentally measured epimutation rates is suspected to be due to model violations.
source: Additionally, we suspect those model violations to explain the discrepancy between the epimutation rates we inferred and the ones measured experimentally (van der Graaf et al., 2015; Denkena et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observed discrepancies.

claim: An Ising model is suggested as a possible way forward for modeling epimutations to account for heterogeneous methylation processes.
source: We thus suggest a possible way forward for modeling epimutations through an Ising model (Zhang et al., 2018) to account for the heterogeneous methylation process.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for future methodological development.

claim: An Ising model generates non-homogeneous mutation process in space and time, violating current SMC assumptions.
source: However, our preliminary work and the simulation results in Briffa et al., 2023, indicate that such model generates non-homogeneous mutation process in space (i.e. along the genome) and time, violating our current SMC assumptions (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: This is based on preliminary analyses and cited simulation results.

claim: There is a need to develop a more realistic methylation model for epimutations.
source: Hence, there is a need to develop a more realistic methylation model for epimutations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observed limitations of current models.

claim: The distance of LD decay for SMPs matches quite well the estimated distance between recombination events.
source: Interestingly, the distance of LD decay for SMPs matches quite well the estimated distance between recombination events (Figure 4).
evidence: This is observed by comparing LD decay patterns to recombination event spacing in Figure 4.

claim: A restricted focus on segregating SMPs in genic regions could meet model assumptions reasonably well.
source: Nonetheless, we find that a restricted focus on segregating SMPs in genic regions could meet our model assumptions reasonably well, and thus provides a promising way forward.
evidence: This is inferred from the better fit of SMPs compared to DMRs to model assumptions.

claim: Using segregating SMPs, a past demographic bottleneck followed by an expansion is recovered which could fit the post-Last Glacial Maximum colonization of Europe.
source: Using these segregating SMPs, we recover a past demographic bottleneck followed by an expansion which could fit the post- Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) colonization of Europe (although caution must be taken concerning the reliability of those results as pointed above), a hypothesized scenario (François et al., 2008) which could not be clearly identified using SNPs only from European (relic and non-relic) accessions (Cao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 and compared to previous SNP-only studies.

claim: Current results for A. thaliana demography are limited by theoretical frameworks unable to simultaneously account for extensive background selection, population structure, and variation in molecular rates.
source: Indeed, beyond the limits of using SNPs only, current results are limited by theoretical frameworks unable to simultaneously account (and disentangle) for extensive background selection (reinforced by very high selfing), population structure and variation in molecular rates (e.g. mutation rates, Monroe et al., 2022), which are all known to be present in A. thaliana.
evidence: This is a known limitation in the field supported by citations.

claim: Various evolutionary forces are known to bias inference results when not accounted for.
source: Those various forces are known to bias inference results when non-accounted for (Charlesworth and Jensen, 2023; Rodríguez et al., 2018), and may explain the variance in our demographic estimates.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on inference biases.

claim: Using CG methylated sites in genic regions may be problematic because typical genealogies at these loci could be shorter than the genome average due to background selection.
source: We also note that using CG methylated sites in genic regions may be problematic as the typical genealogies at these loci could be shorter than the genome average due to the presence of background selection, thus making the inference of such short TMRCA more difficult (even with SMPs) than in non-coding regions (which do not harbour desirable CG methylation sites, van der Graaf et al., 2015; Vidalis et al., 2016; Yao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on known effects of background selection and supported by citations.

claim: Simultaneously accounting for multiple heritable markers can help disentangle different evolutionary forces, such as between selection and variation in mutation rate.
source: We suggest that simultaneously accounting for multiple heritable markers can help disentangle different evolutionary forces, such as between selection and variation in mutation rate: selection has a local effect on the population genealogy, while the mutation rate variation would only locally affect that given marker but not the genealogy (Charlesworth and Jensen, 2023).
evidence: This is a theoretical suggestion supported by a citation.

claim: The absence of conflicting demography inferred from SNPs and from methylation confirms that at the time scale of thousands of generations, CG methylation sites are mainly heritable.
source: The absence of conflicting demography inferred from SNPs and from methylation confirms at the time scale of thousands of generations, CG methylation sites are mainly heritable and can be modeled using population genetics theory (Charlesworth and Jain, 2014; Vidalis et al., 2016 but see Pisupati et al., 2023) and used to estimate divergence between lineages (Yao et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency of demographic estimates and supported by citations.

claim: Fast ecological local adaptation and response to stresses may likely not be prominent forces endlessly reshaping CG methylation patterns.
source: In other words, fast ecological local adaptation (Schmid et al., 2018) and response to stresses (Srikant and Drost, 2020) may likely not be prominent forces endlessly reshaping CG methylation patterns (non-heritability in Figure 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency of demographic estimates and supported by citations.

claim: The approach provides inference tools to study markers' rates and distribution process along the genome without requiring additional experimental data when evolutionary mechanisms are not well understood.
source: If the epimutations/genomic markers evolutionary mechanisms are not well understood (Pisupati et al., 2023; Briffa et al., 2023; Lyons et al., 2023), our approach provides inference tools to study the markers' rates and distribution process along the genome, without requiring additional experimental data.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ability to estimate mutation rates shown in Table 1.

claim: When the evolution of epimutations/genomic markers is well understood and can be modeled, these can be integrated to improve SMC performance.
source: If the evolution of epimutations/genomic markers are well understood (including a measure of the mutation rates) and can be modeled to describe the observed intra-population diversity, these can be integrated to improve the SMC performance.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5B and D where known rates improve inference.

claim: When applying the approach to genome-wide genetic and epigenetic data, it is advisable to use accurately annotated markers with information regarding their inheritance and mutational properties.
source: Hence, when applying our approach to genome-wide genetic and epigenetic data, it is advisable to use accurately annotated markers with, if possible, information regarding their inheritance and mutational properties.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the observed importance of accurate marker characterization.

claim: The set of gene body methylated genes are likely the optimal choice for methylation analysis.
source: Regarding methylation specifically, while the set of gene body methylated genes previously used (Vidalis et al., 2016; Yao et al., 2023) are likely the optimal choice (Yao et al., 2021), these are too few and too scattered across the genome to maximize the statistical power of SMC methods.
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies and practical considerations.

claim: Despite the wealth of functional studies and data on methylation in A. thaliana, the distribution of epimutations is not fully understood.
source: Yet, despite the wealth of functional studies and data on methylation in A. thaliana, the distribution of epimutations is not fully understood (Hazarika et al., 2022; Pisupati et al., 2023), but independent rates for sites and region-level have been estimated (van der Graaf et al., 2015; Denkena et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies highlighting knowledge gaps.

claim: When accounting for region-level epimutations, the algorithm requires first inferring the methylation status of a region via an HMM to later compute epimutation probabilities.
source: When accounting for region-level epimutations, our algorithm requires first inferring via an HMM the methylation status of a region in order to later on compute the epimutation probabilities (i.e. the emission matrix of the SMC HMM).
evidence: This describes the algorithmic approach used in the method.

claim: In the presence of site and region-level epimutations occurring at similar rates, recovering the region methylation status becomes harder.
source: Hence, in the presence of site and region-level epimutations occurring at similar rates, recovering the region methylation status becomes harder as methylated sites are observed in the unmethylated regions (and unmethylated sites observed in the methylated regions).
evidence: This is an inference about the algorithmic challenge based on the nature of the data.

claim: Mislabeling of the region methylation status leads to accuracy loss due to the use of wrong emission probability at later steps of SMC inference.
source: The mislabelling of the region methylation status lead to accuracy loss due to the use of the wrong emission probability at the later steps of the SMC inference (Forward-Backward algorithm).
evidence: This explains the mechanism of accuracy loss observed in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: When epimutation rates are freely inferred, their values are based on the estimated methylation region status and are sufficiently consistent to contain information and slightly improve inference accuracy.
source: When epimutation rates are freely inferred, their values are based on the estimated methylation region status. Therefore, even if the inferred rates are incorrect, these are sufficiently consistent with the inferred region methylation status to contain information and slightly improve inference accuracy.
evidence: This explains the results in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 where unknown rates still improve inference.

claim: Extra care must be taken when dealing with epigenomic data in other species due to potential differences of methylation between different tissues or pools of cells.
source: Additionally, extra care must be taken when dealing with epigenomic data in other species as the SMP calling might not be as simple as for Arabidopsis thaliana due to potential difference of methylation between different tissues or pool of cells.
evidence: This is a cautionary note based on known biological variation in methylation.

claim: The potential dependence between SNPs and SMPs is ignored in the current analysis.
source: Similarly, we ignore here the potential dependence between SNPs and SMPs, as more empirical evidence (and modeling) is required to quantify the potential interaction between both mutational processes.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of a modeling assumption.

claim: With new sequencing technology, long and accurate reads are becoming accessible, leading to high-quality reference genomes for model and non-model species.
source: On a brighter note, with the release of new sequencing technology (Lang et al., 2020), long and accurate reads are becoming accessible, leading to the availability of highquality reference genomes for model and non-model species alike (Nurk et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent technological advances.

claim: The quality of re-sequencing genome data and their annotations is enhanced so that additional markers can be called with increasing confidence.
source: Additionally, the quality of re-sequencing (population sample) genome data and their annotations is enhanced so that additional markers such as transposable elements, insertion, deletion or microsatellites can be called with increasing confidence.
evidence: This is a statement about ongoing technological improvements in the field.

claim: In the near future, there will be an improvement in understanding of the heritability of many markers besides SNPs.
source: We therefore suspect that, in the near future, there will be an improvement in our understanding of the heritability of many markers besides SNPs.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction about future research developments.

claim: Adding other genomic markers besides SNPs will improve full genome approaches, which are currently limited by observed nucleotide diversity.
source: Adding other genomic markers besides SNPs will improve full genome approaches, which are currently limited by the observed nucleotide diversity (Kelleher et al., 2019; Speidel et al., 2019; Schweiger and Durbin, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on current limitations and the results of this study.

claim: The potential complexity resulting from integrating multiple independent markers could be tackled by the use of continuous time Markov chains for the emission matrix.
source: Additionally, the potential complexity resulting by integrating multiple independent markers could be tackled by the use of continuous time Markov chains for the emission matrix.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for methodological improvement.

claim: The results pave the way to improve inference of biological traits or recombination rate through time.
source: We predict that our results pave the way to improve the inference of (1) biological traits or recombination rate through time (Deng et al., 2021; Strütt et al., 2023), (2) multiple merger events (Korfmann et al., 2024), and (3) recombination and mutation rate maps (Barroso et al., 2019; Barroso and Dutheil, 2023).
evidence: This is a speculative prediction about future applications supported by citations.

claim: The method should help dissect the effect of evolutionary forces on genomic diversity.
source: Our method also should help to dissect the effect of evolutionary forces on genomic diversity (Johri et al., 2022; Johri et al., 2021), and to improve the simultaneous detection, quantification and dating of selection events (Albers and McVean, 2020; Bisschop et al., 2021; Johri et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative prediction about future applications supported by citations.

claim: Extending this work by simultaneously integrating diverse types of genomic markers into other theoretical frameworks likely represents the future of population genomics.
source: Hence, there is no doubt that extending our work, by simultaneously integrating diverse types of genomic markers into other theoretical framework (e.g. ABC approaches), likely represents the future of population genomics, especially to study species for which many thousands of samples cannot be obtained.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the future direction of the field.

claim: The approach helps develop more general classes of models capable of leveraging information from any type and amount of diversity observed in sequencing data.
source: We believe our approach helps to develop more general classes of models capable of leveraging information from any type and amount of diversity observed in sequencing data, and thus to challenge our current understanding of genome evolution.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader impact of the methodological framework.
